before: Early model measurements may help allocate limited inspection effort to classifiers that later exhibit subgroup failures despite healthy source performance. We investigate layer-wise connection sensitivity as an additional signal for this decision. GradientGuard summarises the distribution of absolute weight–mean-gradient products across shallow and deep network blocks during the first ten percent of training. A staged investigation combines analytical implementation checks, saved-checkpoint probe-partition analysis, a completed outcome experiment with 96 classifiers in 24 configuration families, and post-hoc diagnostics of frozen forecasts. The source-normal held-out cohort contains 36 classifiers and 12 terminal worst-group failures. Six non-slope layer summaries increase average precision from 0.775 to 0.934 and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.816 to 0.962 relative to the selected conventional predictor. At twelve inspections, both six- and eight-feature layer variants discover ten failures, compared with eight for conventional and global-sensitivity predictors; this pattern persists across the two probe-panel variants examined. At the original nine-inspection endpoint, all four predictors discover eight failures. Whole-family uncertainty includes zero improvement, and one influential-family omission reverses the larger-capacity comparison. The two added layer-share slopes reach the estimator but add no discovery benefit to the six-feature variant in the primary cohort. These results identify non-slope layer summaries as a promising candidate for independent validation while bounding current claims to an exploratory, benchmark-specific association.
after: Early model measurements may help prioritise classifiers for later subgroup-failure audits despite healthy source performance. GradientGuard summarises the allocation of absolute weight-mean-gradient products across network blocks during the first ten percent of training. Analytical and numerical checks establish measurement correctness. An exploratory outcome pilot trained 96 classifiers in 24 setting families. Its source-normal held-out cohort has 36 classifiers and 12 failures: six non-slope layer summaries raise average precision from 0.775 to 0.934, but paired-family ranking intervals include zero improvement and the original nine-audit discovery comparison is tied. A subsequent matched structural-control analysis reuses those outcomes and yields only a panel-dependent increment. A separately frozen fresh-family validation planned 256 classifiers in 64 new families; 248 completed and eight were unavailable because fixed source constructions failed generator validation. Among 106 source-normal evaluation classifiers with 34 failures, a rich structural predictor and the same predictor augmented with six sensitivity shares both discover 26 failures in 35 audits. Their average-precision difference is 0.0005 (95% paired-family interval -0.0057 to 0.0096); AUROC and Brier differences also include zero. Smaller-control and secondary-capacity gains remain, while the sensitivity-specific primary benefit is not demonstrated. The contribution is a reproducible, benchmark-specific evaluation with explicit structural controls and a bounded negative validation result.

before: This article reports a completed exploratory investigation. A measurement-feasibility study established numerical correctness and useful between-run level variation. A targeted follow-up examined probe partitions, classifier-head aggregation and source-health calibration. A separately authorised outcome proof of concept then trained 96 classifiers to completion. Finally, a bounded post-hoc analysis examined the entire capacity curve and the contribution of slopes without fitting new forecasters. We preserve this chronology: the original outcome experiment designated the eight-feature variant L8 and a 25% audit capacity as primary, whereas the present interest in L6 and twelve inspections was sharpened after observing those results.
after: This article reports a staged investigation. Measurement feasibility and a targeted probe/calibration follow-up precede an exploratory 96-classifier outcome pilot and post-hoc capacity/slope diagnostics. The original pilot designated L8 and 25% audit capacity as primary. Its L6 and one-third-capacity observations informed a subsequent reused-outcome structural-control study and then a separately frozen fresh-family validation. The latter tests a matched structural pair at one-third capacity; it does not retrospectively replace the pilot endpoint. We report both the original favourable observations and the completed validation that did not establish the sensitivity-specific primary benefit.

before: The strongest positive observation is that six layer endpoint, mean and spread features improve held-out ranking metrics and discover two additional failures at twelve inspections. The same layer variants recover all twelve observed failures by seventeen inspections, compared with twenty-five for the conventional predictor. These capacity findings are retrospective and motivate fresh validation. The original nine-audit result remains a tie, and the apparent improvement is sensitive to setting-family composition.
after: The pilot layer variants find ten failures at twelve inspections versus eight for conventional/global predictors, but the original nine-audit result is tied and family uncertainty is substantial. In the fresh validation, the rich structural predictor M and its sensitivity-augmented counterpart MZ each find 26 of 34 failures at 35 inspections. Thus the pilot motivates a hypothesis that the stronger test does not support at its predefined primary decision. This negative result narrows the claim from a sensitivity-specific forecasting advance to a reproducible evaluation of a candidate representation.

after: We report conventional, global-sensitivity, norm-product and rich structural controls under matched early information, family folds, preprocessing, learner classes and tuning allowances.

before: We use preserved forecasts to identify which parts of the representation warrant further study: endpoint and prefix-distribution summaries show encouraging exploratory value, while added directional slopes do not improve primary-cohort discovery.
after: We combine frozen-prediction ablations, paired-family ranking intervals and a fresh-family matched validation, retaining ties, losses, unavailable constructions and the unmet sensitivity-specific primary gate.

before: Table 1 makes the comparison boundary explicit. The distinction is an experimentally testable information contract, not a priority claim for all early layer statistics. Three claims must remain separate: layer allocation adds audit value; coordinate-product sensitivity adds value beyond simpler layer statistics; and that increment justifies its monitoring cost. after: Table 1 states the information boundary relative to close prior work; distinct targets alone do not establish superiority. Historical audited models remain necessary for predictor training. The first has some secondary evidence, the fresh primary specificity comparison is tied, and the third remains unestablished.

after: The pilot yielded encouraging non-slope layer-summary rankings, with two extra discoveries at twelve inspections and consistent probe variants. before: The directional interpretation is different. Means and spreads are still summaries of a training prefix; the present findings do not establish that endpoint profiles alone suffice, or that all temporal information is unhelpful. after: The pilot two-slope extension reaches the fitted L8 estimator but does not improve its discovery curve over L6. This does not imply that all history is unhelpful. Endpoint, prefix-distribution and directional information remain distinct questions.

before: Sensitivity-specific originality also remains a testable hypothesis. Existing work already uses early telemetry, weights, gradients, saliency totals and layer-aware aggregation. after: The strongest structural alternative is now an executed comparison. M includes conventional/global information, norm-product allocation, layer weight/mean-gradient marginals and shared bias diagnostics; MZ adds exactly Z. Separate regularisation selection is part of the matched learning procedure, not a pure coefficient intervention. M has 186 inputs relative to 107 eligible fresh development models, so dimensionality and bounded learners remain limitations. before: The main statistical constraint is family diversity. The held-out source-normal set has only three failure-bearing families and no mixed-outcome family. Shared MNIST and outcome panels add dependence beyond repeated seeds. The bootstrap describes a small frozen-predictor setting mixture, and the influential-family reversal prevents interpreting the two-discovery point estimate as a reliable generalisation improvement. The intended primary generalisation is ranking models from previously unseen setting families within the studied benchmark, not necessarily distinguishing initialisation seeds within one setting. Homogeneous outcomes within each eligible family prevent assessing the latter, but do not by themselves invalidate the former. A future design should seek adequate development outcome support and precision before spending its final evaluation budget, without replacing unfavourable families or tuning cutoffs after outcomes. Mixed-outcome families are informative diagnostics, not a requirement imposed retrospectively on every setting.
after: The pilot has only three failure-bearing eligible evaluation families and no mixed-outcome eligible family. The fresh study improves support to twelve failure-bearing and twenty non-failure-bearing eligible families, including four mixed-outcome families, but still shares MNIST identities and outcome panels. Whole-family resampling preserves nested constructions and initialisations; it does not quantify arbitrary dataset shift or forecaster-selection uncertainty. The fresh interval spanning zero is not an equivalence proof. Missing extreme-alignment constructions further condition the result on the available pool.

before: GradientGuard provides a reproducible framework for examining early layer-wise connection sensitivity as a signal for subgroup-audit prioritisation. The completed studies establish engineering correctness of the intended measurement and identify an encouraging non-slope layer-summary pattern in a controlled outcome experiment. In the source-normal held-out pool, L6/L8 improve ranking metrics and find ten failures at twelve inspections compared with eight for conventional/global predictors, with consistent panel checks. The original nine-audit comparison remains a tie, family uncertainty includes zero gain and the added slopes do not improve primary discovery. The next scientific opportunity is a separately frozen evaluation of the six-feature representation against stronger structural alternatives and on a second benchmark context. The present contribution is exploratory evidence and a reproducible test bed for that question.
after: GradientGuard provides a reproducible framework for measuring early layer-wise connection sensitivity and testing its value for subgroup-audit prioritisation. The exploratory pilot shows favourable non-slope ranking point estimates but an original primary discovery tie and wide paired-family uncertainty. Matched norm-product and rich structural controls weaken a sensitivity-specific interpretation. In the separately frozen fresh-family validation, MZ and M both discover 26 failures in 35 audits among 106 source-normal classifiers; ranking/probability difference intervals include zero. Smaller-control and secondary gains remain bounded observations. The completed evidence establishes measurement correctness and a transparent negative primary specificity result within SpuCoMNIST, without demonstrating causal shortcut detection, cross-benchmark transfer or operational savings.
